title: Comparing Philadelphia solos with Bechet and Armstrong
summary: Asked whether the Miller band's solos matched Bechet and Armstrong, Waters says no: they were pioneers and Bill Lee and he were not as good, though he could always improvise.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Some of the first solos, conceived, improvised jazz solos that we recognize as such now, that we can learn about - those of us who weren't there then - through records, seem to indicate to us that the people who were really doin' it, maybe the only ones who were doin' it at first, were Sidney Bechet and Louis Armstrong on the disc. 'Course it was King Oliver, at least for that matter there was Frankie Trumbauer, Johnny Dodds. When you say they were taking jazz solos as we would recognize them today as jazz solos - yourself, Driver, Bill Lee - were they on a par with or relatable to the music of Bechet and Armstrong from the same period music? You must have, wouldn't you hear Bechet the early '20's?
Well, could you compare the solos of the Charlie Miller personnel in 1918, when you're 16 years of age playing with them, with the solo work of Bechet and Armstrong?

No, I wouldn't say that. I tell you why, see. Because actually as we all know Sidney Bechet and - pioneered on the soprano, he was way ahead, and we all know that Louis Armstrong pioneered on the trumpet, way ahead. They wasn't as good, Bill wasn't as good as Louis Armstrong, and I wasn't as good as Sidney Bechet. Well, because I was playing alto, I didn't have the same horn, see.
